bodies.body: This chapter is the map of the notebook, not a full Bosnian grammar lesson. You may already know Ana's Book 1 line Želim kahvu, which means I want coffee. That line is the same drink as kahva, with a different ending because the job in the sentence changed. When you close this page you should know what this book will teach later, and what it will wait on. English hides the work in little words like the and to. Bosnian hides it on the end of words like coffee.

English lies because it keeps the word coffee the same in every job. You can say this is coffee and I want coffee without touching a single letter. You already do a tiny version of the Bosnian trick with people when you say I if you do the thing and me if the thing happens to you. Coffee in English never bothers. Bosnian coffee does, so the list word kahva becomes kahvu when Ana wants the drink. That one change is not a tense, and it is not a new pile. It is a preview of work this book will unpack one system at a time.

Book 1 already gave you Ana's line Želim kahvu, which means I want coffee. She does not repeat the list word kahva, because wanting the drink is a different job from naming it. Today you only need the shock that the word changed. The rest of this notebook explains that change in pieces, one system a day, with the same coffee, bridge, and house.

This notebook teaches four big systems, then a last habit about little words, and it refuses to teach them on the same page. Piles file a word as he, she, or leftover. Jobs change the end of a thing-word when you name it, want it, have none of it, give it, or go with it. Matching words like my have to ride with that pile and that job. Doing-words change for time, and for whether the action is finished. Little words like se then sit in second place in the sentence. You will meet each system on its own day, with the same coffee, bridge, and house.

Use this book one system at a time, with a small chart, a few tries, and a check. The same coffee, bridge, house, Ana, and Emir come back in every chapter so you are not memorizing a new grocery list. You can start here without finishing Book 1, and the sentences will still make sense. If you already walked Book 1, you get a bonus because you have already said the line.

The trap is to call every change a tense. Tense is time on a doing-word, like now versus past. Most of the headache is not time. Thing-words change for the job in the sentence, and they also sit in a pile. Those are different systems. Keep the map in your pocket, and wait for one chapter to open one box. Do not ask tomorrow for every ending on one page.

Old English is not a class you missed. It is the English people actually spoke in England about a thousand years ago. Farmers, priests, and kings around Winchester used it. You do not speak it because languages keep changing. Parents slur, kids copy the slur, and after enough centuries the extra endings fall off. A later mix with French in England sped that wearing-down up, so the English in your mouth is the later, simpler version that won.

That older English hung extra letters on the end of a thing-word to show the job, the same habit Bosnian still has. You can still see a scrap of it when you say I if you do the thing and me if the thing happens to you. Coffee lost those outfits, so this is coffee and I want coffee stay the same. Bosnian never fired the endings on kahva. English moved the work off the word. Bosnian left it on.
You now have the map. Chapter 1 files coffee into a pile so later jobs can pick the right ending. That pile is why kahva is a she. You still will not get a seven-job chart tomorrow.
Kahva is the drink English would never change, and this map starts with why Bosnian will.
Kuća is one of the same few words this notebook will reuse while each system waits its turn.
Most is a bridge on the map, and its pile day comes before any job chart.

Today you learn why kahva lives in the she pile, and how to file the next word the same way. The three pile labels are on, ona, and ono: he, she, and leftover. People follow the person, so Emir is on and Ana is ona without a spelling trick. Things follow the last letter of the list word. Filing is the whole job for this chapter. Later jobs will copy whatever pile you pick today, so a wrong pile today wrecks the endings tomorrow.

English lies because it uses he and she for people and it for almost every thing. Your husband is he, your wife is she, and coffee, a bridge, and a city are all it. Bosnian still uses on, ona, and ono for people, and it uses those same words for things. Coffee landed in the she pile, a bridge landed in the he pile, and beer landed in the leftover pile. The drink did not become a woman. The last letter a stuffed kahva into an old club with kuća. The Bosnian word for this is rod, which means gender, and you can forget the school label as long as you remember the piles.

Book 1 already gave you Ana’s line Želim kahvu, which means I want coffee. Ignore the moved letter for one more chapter. The list word is kahva, and that last a is the pile stamp. Kahvu is still coffee in the she pile. Chapter 2 will explain the job that changed the ending. Today you only file kahva as she, because she-pile words take she-pile endings later.

You guess the pile from the last letter of the list word, which is the boring form sitting in a vocab list. A word that ends in a usually belongs to the she pile, such as kahva, kuća, and ulica, because those words joined an old a club. A word that ends in a consonant usually belongs to the he pile, such as most, dan, and hljeb. A word that ends in o or e usually belongs to the leftover pile, such as pivo, more, and Sarajevo. People skip that cheat sheet because Emir is a man and Ana is a woman. Keep the sheet for coffee, and remember the pile is a filing club, not a vibe.

Two words refuse the cheat sheet, and you should memorize them today because they prove the last letter is a guess, not a law. Tata means dad and ends in a, but it is still he, because dad is a man. Auto means car and ends in o, but it is still he, because this loanword joined the he club anyway. Do not argue with them. More pests will show up later, and these two are enough for this chapter.

The trap is to hear kahvu and think the coffee switched piles to he. It did not. Kahva and kahvu are the same she. The a is the pile stamp on the list word. The u is a later job mark for the thing Ana wants. He-pile most will get a different mark in that same job, and leftover-pile pivo will get a different mark again. If you file coffee as he because you heard a u, you will pick the wrong ending forever.

Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester filed things into three piles the way Bosnian still does. Stone sat in the he pile even though a stone is not a man. Sun sat in the she pile. Wife sat in the leftover pile, which is the proof that the pile was a filing club, not a personality. That system wore off in English. You speak the later version. Bosnian kept the three piles.

Coffee is she because kahva ends in a. That a is an old club stamp. Houses and streets already lived in the a club, so a drink whose list word ended in a joined them. The drink is not girly. The last letter did the filing. Later jobs will copy that pile, which is why getting the pile wrong today wrecks the endings tomorrow.

You now know why coffee, the bridge, and beer live in different piles, and that the pile is a filing club. Kahvu did not make coffee a he. Chapter 2 is why Želim kahvu is not Želim kahva, which is naming the coffee versus wanting it. You still will not get a seven-job chart.
Kahva ends in a, so it belongs in the she pile, not because coffee is girly.
Most ends in t, so it belongs in the he pile.
More ends in e, so it belongs in the leftover pile with pivo.

Today you learn why Ana says Želim kahvu instead of Želim kahva. The list word names the coffee. The moved ending marks the coffee as the thing she wants. English keeps coffee still in both jobs. Bosnian dresses the word again. You already filed the piles in Chapter 1. This chapter is only the name-it job versus the want-it job.

English lies because the phrases this is coffee and I want coffee use the same letters. You already do a tiny Bosnian trick with people when you say I if you do the thing and me if the thing happens to you. Coffee in English never bothers. Bosnian coffee does. The list form kahva is the name-it job. Kahvu is the same she-word in the want-it job. Schools call those jobs nominativ and akuzativ. You can keep saying name-it and want-it and still be right.

Book 1 already gave you Ana’s line Želim kahvu, which means I want coffee. Chapter 1 told you to ignore the moved letter for one day. Today that letter is the whole point. Kahva is the list form that names the drink. Kahvu is the want-it form on the same she-word. The pile did not flip to he. The job in the sentence changed.

She-pile words swap that final a for u when they are the thing you want. Kahva becomes kahvu, and kuća becomes kuću, because those words already sit in the she pile from Chapter 1. He-pile things usually keep the list form in that same job, so most stays most when you want the bridge. Leftover-pile words usually keep the list form too, so pivo stays pivo when you want the beer. People who do the wanting stay in the name-it form. Ana želi kahvu keeps Ana still while coffee moves. Learn the she move first. Then notice that most and pivo often look unchanged.

Two pests will trip you today, and both are worth memorizing early. The first pest is saying Želim kahva, which leaves coffee in the name-it form when Ana wants it. The second pest is he-pile people. Emir stays Emir when you name him, but he often becomes Emira when you see him or want him, because people in the he pile take an a in the want-it job. A bridge does not. Do not argue with Emira. Just remember people and things follow different habits in this job.

The trap is to hear kahvu and decide coffee switched piles to he. It did not. The u is a job mark on the same she-word you filed yesterday. The other trap is to force every word to move like kahva. Most and pivo often stay still in the want-it job, and that stillness is still correct. If you rewrite most into a fake she ending, you invent a word nobody said.

Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester hung extra letters on thing-words to show the job in the sentence. You still own a scrap of that habit when you say I if you do the thing and me if the thing happens to you. He and him work the same way. Coffee lost those outfits in later English. You speak the later version.

Bosnian never fired the outfits on kahva. The name-it form and the want-it form are leftover job marks, the same family of work as I and me. Schools call the whole family case. Today you only need two jobs from that family. Tomorrow’s job is the of and none form on the same coffee.

You now know why Želim kahvu is not Želim kahva, and why most and pivo often look unchanged in that same job. Emira was the people pest. Chapter 3 is the of and none job on the same coffee, the line Nema kahve. You still will not get a seven-job chart.
Ana wants the coffee as kahvu, and the ending moved for the want-it job on the same she-word.
Kuća becomes kuću in the want-it job, the same she-pile move you saw on kahva.
Pivo often stays pivo when you want the beer, the leftover stay-still habit beside the she-word move on kahva.

Today you learn the of, from, and none job on the same coffee you already filed and wanted. Amira can say Nema kahve when the pot is empty, and that e is not the want-it u from Chapter 2. English hangs of and from in front as separate words. Bosnian hangs the job on the end again. You get one new outfit on the same small word set.

English lies because a cup of coffee, coffee from Sarajevo, and there is no coffee keep the word coffee still. You only add little words in front. Bosnian moves the ending instead. Kahva becomes kahve in that job. Schools call the job genitiv. You can keep saying of, from, and none and still be right. The pile stays whatever you filed in Chapter 1. Only the job mark changes.

Book 1 already put Emir in Sarajevo with iz Sarajeva, and it already let Ana want more coffee with Želim još kahve. Today those endings get a name. The café line that shows this job is Amira’s Nema kahve, which means there is no coffee. Kahve is still the she-word. It is not kahvu. Wanting the drink and having none of it are different jobs.

She-pile words swap that final a for e in the of, from, and none job. Kahva becomes kahve, and kuća becomes kuće. He-pile words usually add a, so most becomes mosta and auto becomes auta. Leftover-pile words usually turn the last o or e into a, so pivo becomes piva and Sarajevo becomes Sarajeva. Use that form after nema, after iz and od, and when English would say of. Learn kahve first. Then notice mosta and piva follow their own pile habits.

Three pests will trip you today. The first is saying Nema kahva, which leaves coffee in the name-it form when you mean none. The second is grabbing kahvu because Chapter 2 trained your hand for wanting. Kahvu is want-it. Kahve is of, from, and none. The third pest is Emira. You already saw Emira for I see Emir. The same shape often appears for of Emir or from Emir. People in the he pile reuse that look. A bridge does not reuse that look. Most becomes mosta when you mean of the bridge.

The trap is to treat every moved ending as the want-it job. Kahvu and kahve are neighbors, not twins. Ana wants kahvu. Amira has none of kahve. The other trap is to translate English of as a free word you can drop in front of the list form. Šolja kahva is wrong. Šolja kahve puts the of job on the coffee itself. If you keep the list form after nema, iz, or of, you sound like you never changed jobs.

Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester marked of and from on the end of a thing-word. A scrap survived in later English as the possessive s on names, and as of sitting in front. You speak the later version, so coffee itself stays still while of does the work.

Bosnian never fired that older habit on kahva. The e on kahve is a leftover job mark from the same family as name-it and want-it. Schools call the whole family case. Today you only add the of, from, and none job. Tomorrow’s jobs are to, at, and about on the same coffee.

You now know why Nema kahve is not Nema kahva, and why kahvu stays in the want-it column. Iz Sarajeva and šolja kahve use the same of job. Chapter 4 is giving, liking, and in versus into on the same small set. You still will not get a seven-job chart.
Nema kahve puts the of and none job on the coffee, so the ending is e, not the want-it u.
Kuće is the of form of the house, the same she-pile e you saw on kahve.
Iz Sarajeva uses the from job, so leftover Sarajevo becomes Sarajeva.

Today you learn the to, at, and about job on the same coffee and house. Emir can give coffee to Ana, and Ana can already sit in Sarajevo. English hangs to and in in front. Bosnian hangs the job on the end, and it uses one shared outfit for giving to someone and being at a place. You also learn why into the house and in the house are not the same ending.

English lies because the lines I give coffee to Ana and I am in the house keep Ana and house still. Little words do the work. Bosnian dresses the person you give to and the place you sit in. Ana becomes Ani. Kuća becomes kući. Schools split the labels into dativ for to and lokativ for at and about. On these words the ending is usually the same, so you can learn one chart and two English jobs.

Book 1 already parked you in the city with U Sarajevu, which means in Sarajevo. That u on Sarajevu is today’s at job on a leftover place-word. The new twin is giving. Emir says Dajem Ani kahvu, which means I give Ana coffee. Ani is to Ana. Kahvu is still the want-it form from Chapter 2 for the thing being handed over. Two jobs can sit in one short line.

She-pile words swap that final a for i in the to, at, and about job. Kahva becomes kahvi, kuća becomes kući, and Ana becomes Ani. He-pile words usually take u, so most becomes mostu and Emir becomes Emiru. Leftover-pile words usually take u too, so pivo becomes pivu and Sarajevo becomes Sarajevu. Use that form when you give to someone, when liking uses a to-me scrap like mi, when you are in or on a place, and when you talk about a thing. Keep the want-it form for motion into a place.

The big pest is in versus into. Ja sam u kući means I am in the house, with today’s at form. Idem u kuću means I go into the house, with the want-it form from Chapter 2. The little word u stays the same while the house ending shows the job. The second pest is giving to Ana while leaving her as Ana. Dajem Ana kahvu is English word order with a Bosnian costume. She needs the to form Ani. The third pest is thinking to and at need two different endings on these words. They usually share one outfit.

The trap is to hear u and always reach for one ending. U is not the job. The job sits on the next word. Motion into a place wants the want-it form. Being in or at a place wants today’s form. The other trap is to mark the gift and forget the person. In Dajem Ani kahvu, Ani is to Ana, and kahvu is the coffee being given. If you only change coffee, you still missed the to job.

Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester marked to and at on thing-words and on people words. You still own scraps when you say him and them instead of he and they. Coffee and house lost those outfits in later English. You speak the later version.

Bosnian kept the outfits. The to job and the at job often wear the same ending on one word in the singular, which is why Ani and kući feel like one chart with two English uses. Schools still print two labels. Your ear can treat them as one shared suit until a later chapter needs a finer split.

You now know why Ani and kući share an outfit for to and at, and why into still borrows the want-it form. U Sarajevu and Dajem Ani kahvu are the same family. Chapter 5 adds with and calling, then hangs one preposition map for the whole job set. You still will not drown in a naked seven-row dump.
Dajem Ani kahvu marks Ana with the to form Ani while coffee stays in the want-it form as the gift.
Ja sam u kući uses the at form, while Idem u kuću keeps into on the want-it ending.
U Sarajevu is the at form Book 1 already used for being in the city.

Today you finish the thing-word jobs with with and calling, then you hang one map for the little words that pick those jobs. S kahvom means with coffee, and Emire is how you call Emir across the café. English hangs with in front and uses a bare name to shout. Bosnian dresses both, then gives you one chart that points each English habit at a job you already learned.

English lies because with coffee and hey Emir keep coffee and Emir almost still. You add with, or you just raise your voice. Bosnian moves the ending again. Kahva becomes kahvom after s. Emir becomes Emire when you call him. Schools call those jobs instrumental and vokativ. You can keep saying with and calling. The map at the end is not a new pile. It is a street index for the jobs from Chapters 2 through 5.

Book 1 already called Emir by name with Emire, koliko je sati, which means Emir, what time is it. That e on Emire is today’s calling mark on a he-pile person. The new twin is with. Amira can say Dolazim s kahvom, which means I am coming with coffee, when the cup travels with her. Kahvom is still she. It is not kahvu and not kahve.

She-pile words swap that final a for om in the with job. Kahva becomes kahvom, and kuća becomes kućom. He-pile words usually take om too, so most becomes mostom and Emir becomes Emirom. Leftover words usually take om or em, so pivo becomes pivom and more becomes morem. Put s or sa in front when English says with. The calling job is smaller than the with job. Emir becomes Emire, Ana often becomes Ano, and Amira often becomes Amiro. Learn s kahvom and Emire first. Then read the map so each little word points at the right older job.

Three pests will trip you today. The first is S kahvu, which grabs the want-it form after with. With needs kahvom. The second is calling Emir while leaving him as Emir in a shout across the room. The calling form is Emire. The third pest is treating the map as seven new endings to memorize today. The map only points. U plus into still means the want-it job. Nema still means the of job. S still means the with job. Read the pointer. Reuse the outfit you already own.

The trap is to invent a fresh ending every time you see a preposition. Prepositions are pickers. They do not invent a parallel language. S picks with. Iz picks from. U picks into or in, and the next ending tells you which. The other trap is to mix calling with to. Emire is for calling him. Emiru is for giving to him. If you hand coffee to Emire, you used the shout form in the give line.

Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester had a with outfit on thing-words and a special calling form on names. Later English mostly dropped both on nouns. You kept with as a free word, and you call people with bare names plus tone of voice. You speak that later version.

Bosnian kept both marks. Instrumental is the with and by-means outfit. Vocative is the calling outfit. The map in this chapter is just honesty about prepositions. In older English the ending did more of the pointing. In your English the little word does more of the pointing. Bosnian still lets the ending finish the job the little word started.

You now have with and calling, and one map that points iz, nema, u, na, o, and s at the jobs from Chapters 2 to 5. Coffee still lives in the she pile. The outfits are the only news. Chapter 6 is matching words like my that have to ride with kahva when the job changes. The notebook moves from endings on the noun to endings on the words that stick to it.
S kahvom puts the with job on coffee, so the ending is om, not the want-it u.
Friends raise glasses with company, the same with job you hear in s Emirom and s Anom.
The preposition map only points. Each little word sends you back to a job you already own.

Today you learn why Ana says moja kahva when she names her coffee, and moju kahvu when she wants that same coffee. Matching words like my have to ride with the pile and the job on the thing-word. English keeps my still in every job, while Bosnian dresses my again for coffee, a bridge, or beer. Chapters 1 through 5 filed the piles and the jobs. This chapter is only the matching ride on the same small word set.

English lies because my coffee stays my coffee in every job. You say this is my coffee and I want my coffee with the same my. Bosnian matching words copy the pile first, so coffee takes a she form of my, a bridge takes a he form, and beer takes a leftover form. Then those matching words copy the job too, so name-it moja kahva becomes want-it moju kahvu on the same she-word. Schools call these matching words pridjevi, which means adjectives, and the my set is the possessive kind. You can keep saying matching words and still be right.

Book 1 already gave you Ana’s line Volim moju sobu, which means I love my room. The room is a she-word in the want-it job, so my became moju to ride with it. Today you put that same ride on coffee, the house, the bridge, and beer. Moja kahva names the drink with she-matching my. Moju kahvu wants that same drink, and my moves again with the job.

You pick the matching form from the pile of the thing-word, then dress it for the job. She-pile coffee takes moja in the name-it job and moju in the want-it job, so moja kahva and moju kahvu stay in the she club together. He-pile bridge usually takes moj, and that moj often stays still in the want-it job on a thing, so moj most looks the same when you name it or want it. Leftover-pile beer takes moje, and moje pivo usually stays still in that same want-it job. Descriptive matching words follow the same ride, so lijepa kahva becomes lijepu kahvu when Ana wants the nice coffee. Learn the my set on coffee first. Then notice most and pivo often keep one matching shape.

Two pests will trip you today, and both come from freezing my in English shape. The first pest is saying Želim moja kahva, which leaves my and coffee stuck in the name-it forms instead of moju kahvu. The second pest is saying moj kahva or moje kahva, which grabs the wrong pile because coffee is she. Book 1 already showed you the pile ride on people when Ana said Emir je moj prijatelj and Emir answered Ana je moja prijateljica. Copy the pile you already filed, and do not invent a fresh my for every noun.

The trap is to hear moju and decide my somehow became a he word. It did not. Moja and moju are the same she-matching my on the same she-word coffee. The a marks the name-it job. The u marks the want-it job. The other trap is to move moj most into a fake moju most because coffee moved. He things and leftover words often keep one matching shape in that job, just as most and pivo often kept still in Chapter 2.

Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester made matching words copy the pile and the job of the thing-word. A good man and a good woman did not keep one frozen good the way modern English does. That copying wore off in later English. You speak the later version, where my and nice stay still beside coffee.

Bosnian never fired the matching ride. Moja kahva and moju kahvu are leftover copies of pile and job, the same family of work as the endings on kahva itself. Schools may call the ride agreement, which means the endings have to match. Today you only need the plain fact that my has to dress with coffee, not sit in English pajamas beside it.

You now know why moja kahva becomes moju kahvu, and why moj most and moje pivo often keep one shape in that same job. Matching words ride with the pile and the job. Chapter 7 is mene versus me, and why kod mene needs the long form. You still will not get a seven-job chart.
Moja kahva names the coffee with she-matching my, and moju kahvu wants that same drink.
Moja kuća and moju kuću take the same she-matching ride you just saw on coffee.
Moj most shows the he match, and that matching shape often stays still when you want the bridge.

Today you learn why Bosnian has a long me and a short me, and why a little word like kod forces the long one. English already splits I and me. Bosnian splits me again into mene and me. Book 1 already gave you Amira saying kahvu kod mene. That long form after kod is the whole point today.

English lies because it only keeps one me after I. You say she sees me and coffee at my place without a second outfit for me. Bosnian keeps a full form and a short form for the same job. The short form leans on the doing-word, like me in Vidi me. The full form stands on its own, like mene when you need stress or when a little word such as kod sits in front. Schools call these words zamjenice, which means pronouns. You can keep saying long me and short me and still be right.

Book 1 already gave you Amira’s line Danas pijemo kahvu kod mene, which means today we drink coffee at my place. Kod is a little word that sits in front of the person. After that little word Bosnian needs the long form mene, not the short me. Today you contrast that line with short me after a doing-word, and you keep the same coffee on the table.

Use short me when it can lean on the doing-word, and use long mene when it must stand alone or follow a little word in front. Vidi me means see me, and the short form rides behind the doing-word. Kod mene means at my place, and the long form follows kod. The same split shows up on you as te versus tebe, and on him as ga versus njega. Ja versus mene or me is only a light pointer back to name-it versus want-it, not a second case lesson. Learn ja, mene, and me first on the coffee lines. Then copy the same long-versus-short habit onto ti.

Two pests will trip you today. The first pest is saying kod me, which tries to hang the short form after a little word that needs the long one. The second pest is saying Vidi mene every time, which is not always wrong for stress, but it sounds heavy when short me is the everyday lean. Book 1 also gave you Boli me glava for a short me that leans on the doing-word. Keep kod mene for the little-word line, and keep me for the lean.

The trap is to treat mene and me as two different people. They are the same me in two outfits. The other trap is to borrow English at me and say na me or kod me. After a little word in front, Bosnian wants the long outfit. Short me has nowhere sturdy to lean if the only neighbor is kod or za. That is why Amira says kod mene when the coffee is at her place.

Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester already split I and me for the job in the sentence. You still own that split. Later English mostly stopped making a second, lighter me that could lean on the doing-word.

Bosnian kept both a full form and a lean form. The short ones are little words that prefer second place in the sentence, which Chapter 12 will unpack. Today you only need the coffee-table rule. If a preposition is already sitting in front, grab mene. If the doing-word can carry the lean, me is enough.

You now know why mene and me are the same me in two outfits, and why kod mene needs the long form. Short forms lean on the doing-word. Chapter 8 starts the doing-word map for real, the present tense behind the Book 1 chunks. You still will not get a seven-job chart.
Amira’s coffee at her place needs kod mene, the long form after the little word.
Za mene keeps the long form because za sits in front of me.
Vidi me can use the short form because the doing-word carries the lean.

Today you learn the full now-map for doing-words you already say in pieces. Book 1 gave you želim, volim, and imam as ready chunks. Those endings are the same family on almost every everyday verb. English hangs I, you, and they in front and leaves the verb mostly still. Bosnian hangs the who on the end of the doing-word. This chapter is only the present map. Aspect and past wait for later.

English lies because I want, you want, and they want keep want almost untouched. A tiny s on wants is the whole show for he and she. Bosnian changes the end for nearly every who. Želim is I want. Želiš is you want. Želi is he or she wants. The little words ja and ti are optional once the ending is clear. Schools call this prezent, which means the present. You can keep saying the now-map and still be right.

Book 1 already gave you Ana’s line Želim kahvu, which means I want coffee. That m on želim is the I mark. Emir can say Želiš kahvu when he means you want coffee, and Amira can say Želi kahvu when she means he or she wants coffee. Same verb stem. Different who. Today you stop treating želim as a frozen tourist phrase and start seeing the whole row.

Most everyday verbs take a short who-ending in the present. Ja takes m, so želim and radim. Ti takes š, so želiš and radiš. On, ona, and ono often take a bare ending, so želi and radi. Mi takes mo, and vi takes te. They often take e, as in žele and rade, and some families take ju instead, as in piju from piti. Željeti and raditi are honest samples from the same town words you already know. Keep ja and ti off the page when the ending already says who. Learn the row first, then watch for a few pests that refuse the cheat sheet.

Two everyday verbs refuse the neat row, and you should memorize them early because Book 1 already uses both habits. Ići means to go, but the present is idem, ideš, ide, idemo, idete, idu, not a fake ićim. Biti means to be, and the short present is sam, si, je, smo, ste, su. Saying ja biti or ja ićim invents a tourist form. Do not argue with idem and sam. Just file them beside the regular map.

The trap is to keep saying ja želim as if ja does the real work. The m already marks I. Bosnian often drops ja, ti, and even on when the ending is clear. The other trap is to treat every Book 1 chunk as a frozen postcard. Volim, imam, and govorim are the same who-map as želim. If you invent English-style I want without the Bosnian ending, you erase the whole system this chapter teaches.

Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester hung who-marks on doing-words the way Bosnian still does. Singan could change for I, you, and they. Later English wore most of that off. You kept a scrap in am, is, and are, and a tiny s on wants. You speak the later version.

Bosnian never fired the who-marks on željeti. The present endings are leftover person marks from the same old habit. Schools call the tidy chart prezent. Today you only need the living row on coffee, work, and going. Tomorrow is whether the action is finished, which is a different system on the same verbs.

You now have the present who-map behind želim, radim, and the Book 1 chunks, plus the pests idem and sam. Chapter 9 is why Bosnian often needs two verbs for one English verb, eat versus eat up. The who-endings stay. The finish-line changes.
Želim kahvu puts the I mark on the doing-word, which is the present map behind Ana’s Book 1 line.
Pijem, radiš, and žele are the same who-row on different people at the same table.
Idem is the present of ići, a pest that refuses a fake ićim when someone is going now.

Today you learn why Bosnian often needs two doing-words for one English verb. English says eat for the ongoing plate and for the empty plate, but Bosnian splits that work. Jesti is eat along the way, and pojesti is eat up when the whole thing is done. You already have the present who-map from Chapter 8, and this chapter is only the finish-line. Schools call the split vid, which means aspect, and you can keep saying open versus done and still be right.

English lies because one verb covers both habits. I eat bread can mean a habit, a bite in progress, or a finished meal, and English leans on extra words like up or finished when it cares. Bosnian builds the finish into a second verb, so piti is drink along the way and popiti is drink up. Raditi is work or do along the way, and uraditi is get it done. The pair is not past tense. It is whether the action is open or sealed.

Book 1 already gave you Ana’s line Želim kahvu, which means I want coffee. Wanting sits outside today’s twin pick. When Amira is mid-cup she says Pijem kahvu, which means I am drinking coffee. That is the open twin of piti. The sealed twin is popiti, the drink-it-up verb Emir uses when he says Popij kahvu. Today you only need the shock that piti and popiti are a pair. Past endings wait for Chapter 10.

Think of an open film versus a sealed photo. The open verb covers habits and action in progress, and the sealed verb covers the whole event with a finish line. Coffee uses piti while the cup is open and popiti when the drink is meant to be finished, and bread uses jesti and pojesti the same way. Work uses raditi along the way and uraditi when the job should be done, and going uses ići on the road and otići when leaving is the whole trip. Prefixes like po-, u-, and o- often mark the sealed twin, but you learn pairs, not a fake math rule. Keep the Chapter 8 who-endings on whichever twin you pick, because the finish-line is a different system from who.

Two pests will trip English ears today. The first pest is translating every English present with a sealed verb because it feels more complete. Pijem kahvu is normal for a cup in progress. Popijem kahvu picks the sealed twin and usually looks ahead to a finished cup, not a sip in progress. Popij kahvu is the finish command on that same sealed twin. The second pest is hunting a sealed twin for every word on day one. Some verbs live mostly open, and some pairs you just memorize with coffee and bread. Do not invent fake prefixes. Learn the town pairs first.

The trap is to call the sealed verb past tense. Pojesti is still a doing-word about finishing, not a time machine by itself. Past tense hangs sam and gender endings on top, and that is tomorrow. The other trap is to force English up onto every Bosnian line. Sometimes Bosnian picks the open verb for a habit even when English would say finished. Listen for open versus done, not for a magic English particle.

Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. It cared a lot about time on the verb, and later English kept that habit with will, did, and have. What English mostly lost is a clean pair of verb twins for open versus done. You paper over the gap with particles like up and out. Eat up is a clue, not a full system.

Bosnian kept the twin system. Schools call it vid, which means aspect. Slavic languages treat the finish-line as basic furniture, the way English treats tense. That is why one English eat becomes jesti and pojesti. Today’s coffee and burek are the same objects from Book 1. The new work is picking the twin.

You now know why jesti and pojesti both translate eat, and why the sealed twin is not automatically past. Chapter 10 hangs sam and the gender endings -o, -la, and -lo on those same verbs. Emir was there and Ana was there will finally split on the doing-word.
Jedem burek is the open bite, and pojesti is eat the burek up when the tray is the finish line.
Pijem kahvu keeps the cup open, while popiti seals the same drink as drink up.
Idem na most keeps going open, and otići seals leaving as the whole trip.

Today you learn how Bosnian builds the past with a little helper plus a gendered piece of the doing-word. English says I worked and she worked with the same worked. Bosnian says Radio sam if Emir worked and Radila sam if Ana worked. The helper is sam, si, or je for one person, and the other piece takes -o, -la, or -lo to match who did it. This chapter is only that past.

English lies because the past ending on the doing-word usually ignores whether the speaker is a man or a woman. I cooked and she cooked share cooked. Bosnian hangs gender on the past form itself. Bio is he was. Bila is she was. Bilo is leftover was. Schools call the helper forms of biti, and they call the whole tense prošlost, which means the past. You can keep saying sam plus the gendered piece and still be right.

Book 1 already taught you Ana, Emir, and the short word sam in lines like Ovdje sam. Today that helper joins the past. Emir can say Bio sam u Sarajevu, which means I was in Sarajevo. Ana can say Bila sam na moru, which means I was at the sea. Same helper family. Different gendered piece because Emir is he and Ana is she. The coffee and the house stay in their Chapter 1 piles. The new work is on the doing-word.

Build the everyday past in two parts. First pick the helper that matches who. Ja takes sam, ti takes si, and on or ona takes je. Then pick the gendered piece of the verb. He-pile who gets -o, as in bio, radio, and pio. She-pile who gets -la, as in bila, radila, and pila. Leftover who gets -lo, as in bilo when pivo or Sarajevo is the subject. The helper can sit in second place, so Bio sam and Ja sam bio both appear. Learn Emir versus Ana first. Then notice leftover ono uses -lo.

Two pests will trip you today. The first pest is matching the past ending to the thing you drank instead of the person who drank. Ana says Pila sam kahvu with -la because Ana is she, not because coffee somehow became she in the past. The second pest is forgetting the helper. Radio without sam is not a finished everyday past for I worked. Keep sam, si, or je in the sentence. Those two habits will save you more grief than any new chart.

The trap is to hear -la and decide the whole sentence flipped into the she pile for every noun. The -la marks who did the action, usually the person. Kahvu can still sit in its want-it form beside that past. The other trap is to copy English and put a he ending on a she speaker. If Ana did it, use radila. If Emir did it, use radio. Leftover subjects take -lo, and that form shows up less in café talk, so master he and she first.

Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. It had richer past forms than yours, but it did not keep a clean he-worked versus she-worked split on the verb the way Bosnian does. Later English locked past on time words and endings like -ed. You speak that later version.

Bosnian past is an old combo. A short piece of to be plus an old verbal adjective that still agrees in gender. That is why Ana and Emir diverge on radila versus radio even when English keeps worked still. Schools may say L-participle once. You only need sam plus the gendered piece. Tomorrow adds the future helper and the everyday can-must-want row.

You now can build Bio sam and Bila sam, and you know the -la follows Ana, not the coffee. Chapter 11 adds the future with ću, blunt versus polite commands, and the everyday row for can, must, and want. You still only own the past from today.
A stroll through town is still Bio sam for Emir and Bila sam for Ana, because the past piece follows who walked.
Pio sam kahvu and Pila sam kahvu split on who drank, not on coffee switching piles.
Išla sam kući keeps -la on Ana, while the house stays the same she-word from earlier chapters.

Today you learn three café tools that travel together. Future uses short ću, ćeš, će, ćemo, ćete, će plus an infinitive, as in Ti ćeš piti kahvu for you will drink coffee. Commands have a blunt form and a polite form, as in Radi versus Radite. Want, must, need, and can sit on htjeti, morati, trebati, and moći. English spreads these across will, please, and helper verbs. Bosnian keeps them short. This chapter is that bundle, and clitic second place waits for Chapter 12.

English lies because will, please, can, must, and need feel like separate drawers. You will drink, drink please, you must drink, and you can drink each grab different helpers and tones. Bosnian reuses a tiny future helper, a command ending, and four everyday modal verbs. Hoću overlaps with wanting. Moram is I must. Trebam is I need. Mogu is I can. Schools may split budućnost, imperativ, and modalni glagoli onto three posters. In this notebook they share one day because you meet them in the same café turn.

Book 1 already gave you Ana’s line Želim kahvu, which means I want coffee. Wanting also rides on htjeti, so Hoću kahvu is a blunt cousin you will hear. Emir can answer Ja ću piti kahvu when he means I will drink coffee. Amira can soften a command to Molim, radite or keep it blunt with Radi. Today you map those moves without inventing English word-for-word copies.

Future is a short helper plus an infinitive. Ja ću piti, ti ćeš piti, on će piti, mi ćemo piti, vi ćete piti, oni će piti. The helper likes second place, so Ja ću piti kahvu and Piti ću kahvu both appear, and a naked Ću at the start of a sentence is wrong. Commands cut to a short stem for one friend, as in Radi, Pij, and Idi, and they add -te for polite or plural, as in Radite, Pijte, and Idite. The modal row is small. Mogu means I can. Moram means I must. Trebam means I need. Hoću means I want. Keep the Chapter 8 who-endings on those modals, and leave the finish of the action for another day.

Three pests will trip you today. The first pest is stacking English will onto a present form, as in will pijem, or parking ću at the front of the sentence. Use Ja ću piti or Piti ću. The second pest is barking Radi at a stranger when Radite or a soft molim would fit. Blunt is fine with friends. Polite -te is safer with new people. The third pest is mixing trebati and morati. Moram is duty pressure. Trebam is need. Hoću is want, and it is not the same soft wish as želim in every room, even when both translate want.

The trap is to treat ću as optional flavor on a present sentence, or to put ću first. Ja ću piti is future. Pijem is present. Ću piti with nothing before ću breaks the second-place habit Chapter 12 will name. The other trap is to hear Hoću kahvu and decide Bosnian lost želim. Both live. Želim often sounds like a plain want from Book 1. Hoću can sound stronger or more blunt. For commands, do not add please into the verb ending. Molim is a separate softener beside Radite.

Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. It had its own future hacks and command forms, and later English rebuilt future with will and going to. You speak that rebuilt kit. Please stayed a separate soft word, the way molim still sits beside a command in Bosnian.

Bosnian future helpers are worn-down bits of htjeti, the want verb, which is why ću smells like wanting while it marks time. Commands keep an old short stem. The modal row is just high-frequency verbs that take infinitives the way English can and must do. Schools split the posters. Café talk bundles them, so this chapter does too.

You now have ću for tomorrow, blunt versus polite commands, and the café row mogu, moram, trebam, and hoću. Chapter 12 is why little words like se and sam hunt second place in the sentence. Ja se zovem works. Se zovem does not. That habit finishes the grammar walk before the English-shaped mistakes review.
Idite na most is the polite command shape, while Idi stays blunt for one friend.
Ja ću piti kahvu hangs the future on ću in second place plus the infinitive, not on an English will stuck in front of pijem.
Hoću, moram, trebam, and mogu are the short café row for want, must, need, and can.

Today you learn why Ja se zovem Ana works and Se zovem Ana does not. Little words like se, mi, sam, and ću need a seat in second place in the sentence. English lets myself and me wander. Bosnian parks these short words right after the first stressed chunk. Book 1 already gave you Zovem se Ana. This chapter is only that parking rule.

English lies because short words can sit almost anywhere. You can say I call myself Ana, or My name is Ana, and nobody checks the second slot. Bosnian still uses short words for the same jobs, and those short words refuse to open the sentence. Se turns the action back on the speaker in zovem se. Mi means to me in Drago mi je. Sam helps build a past line. Ću helps build a future line. Schools call the short pack enklitike, which means clitics. You can keep saying little words in second place and still be right.

Book 1 already gave you Ana’s meeting line Zovem se Ana, which means my name is Ana. The same rule lets her say Ja se zovem Ana. In both lines se sits in second place. Zovem holds first place in the short version. Ja holds first place when she puts herself up front. Se zovem Ana fails because se tried to open the sentence, and Bosnian will not let that little word start.

Put one stressed word or short phrase first, then park the little word. Ja se zovem Ana puts Ja first and se second. Zovem se Ana puts Zovem first and se second. Drago mi je puts Drago first and mi second. Pio sam pivo puts Pio first and sam second. Ja ću doći puts Ja first and ću second. You may shuffle the big words for stress or style. You may not shove se, mi, sam, or ću into first place. Second place is the whole job for this chapter.

Three pests will trip you today, and all three come from English word order. The first pest is starting with se, as in Se zovem Ana. The second pest is parking the little word at the English end, as in Ja zovem se Ana. The third pest is opening with sam or ću alone, as in Sam pio pivo or Ću doći. Fix them the same way. Put a real first word down, then seat the little word. Zovem se, Pio sam, and Ja ću all clear the rule.

The trap is to think Ja must always sit in the sentence for the rule to work. It does not. Zovem se Ana already has a first place word, so se is happy in second place with no Ja at all. The other trap is to treat every short Bosnian word like a free English pronoun. After a preposition you need the long form from Chapter 7, so za mene stays long while me alone is the short rider for other seats. Today you only lock second place. The long-versus-short chart already had its day.

Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester already liked to cluster small unstressed words early in a clause. Later English loosened that parking habit, so myself and me can wander. You speak the later version.

Bosnian kept a stricter second-place rule for its short pack. Linguists sometimes call the old habit Wackernagel’s law, which just means little words sit in second place. Se in Ja se zovem is the same family of parking. The meaning is not in a free English slot. The seat is the rule.

You now know why Ja se zovem and Zovem se both work, and why Se zovem fails. Little words like se, mi, sam, and ću sit in second place. Chapter 13 is the mixed review of the whole notebook, from piles to this parking rule. There is no new system tomorrow.
At Sebilj Ana says Ja se zovem Ana, and se sits in second place after Ja.
Zovem se Emir also works here because Zovem takes first place and se still parks second.
Drago mi je parks mi in second place, the same second-seat rule as se in zovem se.

Today you walk the whole notebook again without learning a new system. Piles file coffee as she, and jobs dress kahva into kahvu when Ana wants it. Matching words ride with that pile and that job, doing-words mark time and finished action, and little words like se sit in second place. English will still push you toward one wrong habit from each shelf. This chapter names those habits and checks the map.

English lies in five friendly ways at once. It keeps coffee still in every job. It uses he and she for people and it for almost every thing. It lets my stay still while the noun moves. It uses one eat for ongoing and finished action. It lets myself wander to the front of a sentence. Bosnian answers each lie with a different shelf from this book. The mix-up starts when you grab the wrong shelf for the headache in front of you.

Book 1 already gave you Ana’s coffee line Želim kahvu, and Chapter 12 just parked Ja se zovem Ana. Together they carry three systems you now own. Kahva is she from the pile chapter. Kahvu is the want-it job on that same she-word. Se sits in second place after Ja. Today you only rehearse those shelves side by side. You do not open a new chart.

Use the map before you invent a fix. Ask which shelf is broken. If the last letter files the word, you are in piles. If the ending marks name-it, want-it, none-of-it, to-it, or with-it, you are in jobs. If my or big has to copy the noun, you are in matching. If time or finished action moved, you are in doing-words. If a little word tried to open the line, you are in second place. Name one headache, then open one shelf. That is the whole review.

Five pests come back today, one from each shelf. Tata ends in a and still sits in the he pile. Želim kahva leaves coffee in the name-it form. Moja kahvu matches the pile and misses the job. Jesti and pojesti are not free twins for every eat. Se zovem parks the little word in first place. Name the pest, then open the right older chapter. Do not build a sixth system.

The trap is to treat every wrong ending as the same kind of mistake. Kahvu is not a pile change, not a tense, and not a matching failure. It is the want-it job on a she-word you already filed. Se zovem is not a pile problem either. It is a parking problem. If you swing one hammer at every miss, you invent grammar nobody in Sarajevo said.

Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. Farmers and priests around Winchester hung work on the ends of words, filed things into piles, and clustered small words early. Later English moved a lot of that work into little separate words and freer order. You speak the later version.

Bosnian kept more of the older toolkit on the word itself. That is why this notebook needed shelves instead of one mega chart. English speakers go wrong when they expect one English habit to cover five Bosnian jobs. The map is the fix. The coffee stayed the same coffee the whole time.

You now have the whole map in one place. Piles file the word, jobs dress it, and matching words ride along. Doing-words mark time and finished action, and little words sit in second place. There is no Chapter 14 in this handbook. Go back to coffee, the bridge, and Ana when a line feels wrong, and name the shelf before you guess.
Želim kahvu still carries the she pile and the want-it job on the same coffee from Chapter 1 and Chapter 2.
Most stays in the he pile, and Želim most often keeps the list form in the want-it job.
Kuća becomes kuću in the want-it job, the same she-pile move the review keeps asking you to name.
